en: The Essentials of the Chan Gate, composed by the Great Master Tiantai.

This work sets forth the Dharma-gate for cultivating meditation and studying wisdom. First, it clarifies the expedient means; second, it clarifies right contemplation. Regarding the expedient means, for all...
There are five [conditions]. First, there are five requisite factors: (1) the sufficiency of food and clothing; (2) the purity of one's observance of the precepts;
(3) dwelling in a secluded and quiet place; (4) ceasing all worldly activities; and (5) associating with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

If these five factors are lacking, they will obstruct the settling of the mind (*śamatha*). If one lacks a virtuous friend, one will not know how to remove obstacles. It is for this reason [that these conditions are required].
One must possess five conditions.
Second, the censure of the five desires refers to form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. These five can give rise to the practitioner’s mind of sensual pleasure;
through greed and attachment, one knows no satisfaction. If they are not censured and cast aside, they will obstruct right practice; therefore, they must be censured and rejected.
One abandons the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*). These five hindrances are: first, the hindrance of sensual desire; second, the hindrance of ill will; third, the hindrance of sloth and torpor;
fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse; and fifth, the hindrance of doubt. If these five are abandoned, the mind attains tranquility.
When these five reside within the mind, they enshroud and obscure it, preventing clarity.

Regarding the four ways of regulating the five matters: first, regulate food so as to be neither hungry nor overly full; second, regulate the eyes so that they are neither too restricted nor too unrestrained—these two are regulated externally to concentration.
Third, regulate the body; fourth, regulate the breath; fifth, regulate the mind—these three are regulated internally to concentration.
As for regulating the body, making it neither too loose nor too tense is the characteristic of bodily regulation. Next, regarding the regulation of the breath, make it...

The inhalation and exhalation are gentle, still, and subtle, as if they were present and yet absent. This sustains the spirit and stabilizes dhyāna; by maintaining this, it is easy to attain concentration. To state the essentials:

neither constricted nor slippery is the characteristic of regulated breath. Next, regarding the regulation of the mind: if there is excessive discursive thought (*vitarka*) and observation (*vicāra*), or if the mind is restless, one must bind the mindfulness to the navel region to restrain all distracted thoughts.
If the mind is sunken, dull, or the head droops into deep sleep, [one must apply the appropriate remedy].
Regarding that which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): one should fix the tip of the nose, causing the mind to remain upon its object without distraction.

To state the essentials: being neither sunken nor agitated is the characteristic of a balanced mind. Next, while sitting correctly, if one perceives that the three factors—the body, the breath, and the mind—are not in balance, one must immediately employ the aforementioned method to harmonize them.
If these three factors are balanced, meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) can be attained. Next, wishing to...

When emerging from meditative absorption, one should first relax the mind by directing it toward other objects. Next, open the mouth and release the breath, imagining that it disperses freely through the hundred vessels.
Then, move the body very slightly; next, move the shoulder blades, hands, head, neck, and so forth;
next, move both feet, knees, and so forth. Next, rub all the pores of the body with the hands. Finally, press the palms together to warm them and cover both eyes. Thereafter—
Open your eyes. Wait until the sweat on your body has dried before proceeding as you wish; if you do not do so, it will cause illness in people.

Regarding the fifth practice, the five dharmas, they are: desire (*chanda*), diligence (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), skillful wisdom (*prajñā*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*). The commentary states:
"Desire" means desiring to leave behind all worldly delusions and inversions, and desiring to attain all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and wisdoms.

This is a Dharma gate. As for diligence: it is to maintain the purity of the precepts and, throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, to single-mindedly and diligently practice the unsurpassed Dharma of the Path.
As for mindfulness: it is to mindfully attend to the worldly dharmas of livelihood and production; such that not even a single color or a single fragrance is anything other than the Buddha-dharma.
As for skillful wisdom: it is to contemplate the worldly aggregates, elements, and sense bases, so that each and every one enters into reality as it is.
It causes the realm of Māra to be immediately the realm of the Buddha, performing the work of a Buddha just as Sadāprarudita did. As for "single-mindedness":

having realized that worldly dharmas are themselves supramundane dharmas, one should single-mindedly cultivate the two dharmas of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), causing them to accord with the *dharmatā*.
When the mind is like a vajra, such that nothing can destroy it, it is therefore called "single-mindedness. All of the above constitutes seated meditation (*zuo chan*).
This method is briefly indicated by way of its entry and exit. Now, one who wishes to resolve to cultivate the Way must first inquire about the path.

Paths have obstructions and openings; teachings have what is right and what is wrong; and the mind has the deviant and the correct. For now, I shall illustrate their characteristics by taking *zuo-chan* (seated meditation) as the example;

the rest can be understood through this. As for obstructed paths: suffering (*duḥkha*) and its accumulation (*samudaya*) constitute obstructions, while the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) constitute openings. Ignorance (*avidyā*) and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) constitute obstructions.

The extinction of ignorance constitutes the opening; the six obscurations constitute the blockage. The six perfections constitute the opening. If there are these three blockages, one must destroy them to bring about the opening.

Next, to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox: first, if one resolves to study meditation for the sake of gain and offerings, or for such matters as breaking the precepts, this resolution is a mind for the *niraya* hell;
it is the practice of the path to hell. Second, if one seeks fame and relies on the praise of others...

1. Those who practice meditation while giving rise to a deceitful and crooked mind are practicing the way of ghosts. 2. Those who do so for the sake of gaining followers, a large retinue, or patrons are practicing the way of birds and beasts.

3. Those who do so for the sake of their kinsmen and attendants are practicing the way of birds and beasts. 4. Those who do so out of a desire to surpass others and out of envy are practicing the way of the asuras with a hideous mind.
5. Those who do so because they fear losing their future human status after this life passes away are practicing the way of the asuras with a hideous mind.
6. Those who, while maintaining the precepts, resolve their minds to study *dhyāna*, are generating the lower mind of the desire realm; such persons follow the path of humans. 7.

If, for the sake of seeking natural retribution (*vipāka*) in this life or future lives, one practices the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), this is generating the higher mind of the desire realm;
such persons follow the path of devas. 8. If, in order to suppress others and further elevate oneself, one sits like a wolf, stares haughtily, and...
8. If one seeks the meditative concentration, tranquility, and bliss of this life and future lives, this is the arousal of the Brahma-mind;
one practices the path of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). 9.

If one seeks worldly wisdom, eloquence, and the knowledge of all things without exception, and practices meditation for this purpose, this is the arousal of the mind of an outsider (*tīrthika*); one practices the path of the [formless] realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

One should contemplate proceeding along the path of the heavens. Tenth, if one contemplates that the cycle of birth and death within the world is like a prison and is utterly loathsome, and that supramundane *nirvāṇa*—pure and quiescent—is utterly delightful, and for this reason resolves to swiftly escape the three realms, this is the arousal of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and the practice of the path of the two vehicles;
it is not the immeasurable mind. These ten types briefly demonstrate what is not the immeasurable mind.
Listen. The first nine are mundane minds; they are the minds of birth and death. The latter one is the supramundane mind;

it is the mind of nirvana, the mind of the noble ones, and the mind of liberation. Practitioner, as you study and cultivate the path, you should skillfully distinguish between the false and the correct.

Do not rashly give rise to [false] resolve. Even the supramundane path of the Two Vehicles involves distinguishing between right and wrong; how much more so regarding those previous states of mind which were falsely claimed to be correct?

If you wish to accord with principle, simply attend first to human affairs; do not force yourself to know the affairs of others. This will lead to mutual resentment and hatred from lifetime to lifetime.
Not only will there be no Way or fruition in this life, it will afflict future lives as well.
Those who can close their mouths, join their palms, plug their ears, sit upright, and cultivate the mind are world-transcending sages.
If one does not do so, it will be difficult to escape the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.

Next, the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is explained. First, regarding cultivation while seated: the practitioner, amidst the distractions of discursive thoughts and mental investigations during sitting, cultivates the three types of cessation (*śamatha*).
The first is called "cessation by binding the object" (*ālambana-bandhana-śamatha*). This means binding the mind to the tip of the nose, the space between the eyebrows, or other such locations;
by binding the object and guarding the focal point, one prevents the mind from scattering. The second is called "cessation by restraining the mind" (*citta-nigraha-śamatha*). This follows the mind...

If thoughts do not arise, one must immediately restrain them so that they do not scatter. These two are merely the cessation of phenomena (*vastu*). Third is the cessation of realizing the true nature (*tattva*).

This means that according to whatever the mind contemplates, one must realize all dharmas as they are: knowing that they all arise from conditions, and that dharmas arising from conditions possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Once one knows they lack intrinsic nature, one does not grasp at or cling to them; because one does not grasp, [there is cessation].
When the mind of deluded thought ceases, this is called *śamatha* (calm abiding). The unmoving state of the settled mind is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The unconditioned is the source of all phenomena (*dharmas*). If one can settle in this source, then all deluded thoughts, the cycle of birth and death, and karmic activities will become empty and quiescent;

this is the path of *nirvāṇa*, the true and real Dharma. This concludes the brief explanation of the three types of calm abiding. Next, as for the practice of *vipaśyanā* (insight): it is said that...
Right contemplation is the wisdom that perceives the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena through the Middle Way.

When a practitioner is engaged in seated meditation, they observe all phenomena according to whatever the mind takes as its object—whether wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, or indeterminate dharmas—and these objects do not remain fixed from moment to moment.
Even if one has realized the truth as described above, if one does not yet abide therein, one should instead turn back and contemplate the very mind that has arisen.
From where does it arise? Does it arise from the past, the present, or the future? If it arises from the past, since the past has already ceased, how can it produce anything?
If it arises from the present, since the present momentary states do not abide, how can they produce anything?
If it arises from the future, since the future has not yet arrived, how can it produce anything? [Thus it is with] the three times.
Seeking the arising of life, it is ultimately unattainable. One should know that this mind exists only as a name.

The nature of names is fundamentally non-arising. Because it is non-arising, it is non-ceasing; because it is non-ceasing, it is the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is contemplation.
Furthermore, when one examines whether this mind exists or does not exist: if the mind did not exist, how could there be thought? If the mind were...
If it were existent, it should exist inherently; why would it need to arise through conditions before the mind could be produced? One should know that this mind is neither existent nor non-existent;
this is precisely the Middle Way of right contemplation.

Furthermore, if during dhyāna one becomes dull, drowsy, or falls asleep with the head bowed in a state of non-discrimination, one must immediately practice vipaśyanā, discerning the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) as an antidote to the affliction of dullness.
If, while sitting in meditation, the mind becomes distracted, agitated, or strays to grasp at myriad objects, [one must apply the appropriate remedy].

One must immediately employ *śamatha* (calm abiding) to eliminate distracted thoughts and maintain single-minded mindfulness. If, while practicing *śamatha*, the mind is peaceful and joyful, one should continue to practice *śamatha*.
Furthermore, if while practicing *śamatha* one can overcome drowsiness and distraction, one should continue to practice *śamatha*.

Moreover, if while practicing *śamatha* the mind becomes clear and free from sensual desire, one should continue to practice *śamatha*. Likewise, when practicing *vipaśyanā* (insight), if the ground of the mind is tranquil and blissful, it is appropriate to practice [further].
Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, when the mind of the Way (*bodhicitta*) arises with intensity during the practice of contemplation, one should immediately cultivate contemplation.

Moreover, when contemplating enables one to destroy afflictions and evil views, one should immediately cultivate contemplation. If contemplation is beneficial, one should constantly cultivate contemplation; if tranquility (*śamatha*) is beneficial, one should constantly cultivate tranquility.
The practitioner must skillfully deliberate and employ tranquility and contemplation to harmonize the mind, ensuring that deluded thoughts do not arise. Thus...
This is a skillful application of the mind; it possesses a degree of principle.

Next, the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* through traversing conditions and confronting objects is explained. There are six conditions to be traversed: namely, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, and performing tasks.
There are likewise six objects to be confronted: namely, the six sense faculties encountering the six sense objects. Thus, conditions and objects coincide.
There are twelve matters. First, regarding those who cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within the context of walking:
when a practitioner wishes to walk, they should immediately reflect: "For what purpose am I walking now? If it is for an evil matter or a useless matter, one should not walk;
if it is for a wholesome matter or a beneficial matter, one should walk. This is how one cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* while walking. Furthermore—

One should know that because of causes within formations (*saṃskāra*), there exist all phenomena such as good and evil. Now, when one investigates these formations and all phenomena, they are found to be entirely false and illusory;
seeking their reality, it cannot be found, and thus deluded thoughts do not arise—this is called *śamatha*. Furthermore, one forms this thought:
"It is by means of the mind moving the body that there is coming and going, as well as all phenomena within the process of walking. One then proceeds to contemplate these formations.

Within this, one does not perceive the characteristics, the place of coming, or the place of going; there is neither arising nor ceasing. One should know that the practitioner and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent.
This is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Since this is how one cultivates calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) within the conditions of practice, so it is.

The remaining five conditions are analogous to this example. Next, regarding the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā with respect to objects: when seeing a form, one immediately knows it to be like an illusion or a magical transformation and does not give rise to greedy attachment;
the mind is tranquil and still—this is called śamatha. One should then practice vipaśyanā by investigating from where the mind that sees the form arises:
does it arise from the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), or from the form-object (*rūpa-viṣaya*), or from the conjunction of the faculty and the object?

It arises in order to be separated from the sense organs and their objects. If you claim that seeing arises from the eye, then the mind should have already arisen even before the object of form is seen.
If it arises from the objective field of form, what concern is that of mine? If it arises from their conjunction, examine these organs and objects:
do they each possess a mind, or do they each lack a mind? If a mind were able to produce a mind, then at the moment of conjunction there would have to be two minds.

If it were possible for a mind to arise from that which is itself devoid of mind, such a thing could not exist. If a mind were to arise apart from the sense organs and their objects, such a thing could likewise not exist.
One should know that the mind which perceives forms is fundamentally unarisen; it exists only as a name, and the nature of names is empty, ultimately lacking any reality.
This is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Just as this is the case when practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* while seeing forms with the eyes, so it is for all other instances.
The same principle applies to the other five faculties in relation to the five objects.

Next, regarding the practice of the threefold contemplation within a single mind during the worship of the Buddha: one contemplates that the single thought-moment of the mind worshipping the Buddha is simultaneously empty, simultaneously provisional, and simultaneously the Middle Way.

Contemplating the mind as empty is worshipping the *vipāka-buddha* (the Buddha of Retribution); contemplating the mind as provisional is worshipping the *nirmāṇa-buddha* (the Buddha of Transformation).

To contemplate the mind as being itself the Middle Way is to pay homage to the Buddha of the Dharma. One prostration is three prostrations; one Buddha is three Buddhas. Though three, they are one; though one, they are three.
This is called the Perfect Prostration, and it is also called the Inconceivable Prostration to the Buddha.

Furthermore, whether reciting sutras, circumambulating, encountering conditions, facing objects, or when the mind moves and thoughts arise, all should be treated according to this principle: the application of the Three Contemplations. Question: One...

What is the function of the three contemplations of the mind? Answer: The contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) destroys the delusions of the four abodes; the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) destroys the delusions as numerous as motes of dust;

and the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama*) destroys the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*). Through the three contemplations within a single mind, the three truths are perfectly and simultaneously destroyed.

When the five abodes of afflictions are destroyed, the three bodies (*trikāya*) are manifested: when the four abodes are destroyed, the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is manifested; when the delusions as numerous as motes of dust are destroyed, the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is manifested.
The body is manifested. When ignorance is destroyed, the Dharma-body is manifested. Furthermore, because the three contemplations are perfected, the three virtues are fulfilled:

when the Middle Contemplation is perfected, the Dharma-body is fulfilled; when the Contemplation of the Provisional is perfected, Prajñā is fulfilled; and when the Contemplation of Emptiness is perfected, Liberation is fulfilled.
Because these three virtues are fulfilled, it is called the Secret Treasury. Both Buddhas and sentient beings enter into it; ultimately, there is nothing at all. Forever...
It is as tranquil as empty space. If this is so, why further say that there are all dharmas and that the Buddha uses provisional names to guide sentient beings?

Furthermore, although the true dharma of nirvāṇa is such that sentient beings enter it through various gates, I have here briefly set forth this teaching based on a single principle for the sake of beginners, showing them the way;
one must not grasp this as being the only truth to the exclusion of others.
This would be incorrect. If one grasps this meaning, then it is as if a thousand chariots share the same ruts and ten thousand streams all converge.
The essential nature of all dharmas is equal; the Dharmakāya Buddha within the bodies of sentient beings pervades all of space and the entire Dharma-realm.
All practitioners should constantly collect their thoughts and contemplate that the four great elements and the five aggregates are empty and non-existent; this is called the Way.
Essentials of the Chan Gate (End)
